title: Refuge of the bad
hook: the Tao is the treasure of the good and the refuge of the bad (Tao Te Ching 62)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lower river: the great one draws others by lying low. Your line was the low place. Who found you easier to reach? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

Who gets to come back after they've failed? Some households have an answer, and it's a chair at the kitchen table. The cousin who lost the job. The friend who said the unforgivable thing at the wedding. The kid who got suspended. Nobody gives a speech first. Somebody puts down a plate. Chapter sixty-two of the Tao Te Ching says the Way itself works like that table. It belongs to the good, and it also shelters the ones who aren't. Today, refuge of the bad.
screen: `WHO GETS TO COME BACK?` → `A CHAIR, A PLATE, NO SPEECH.` → `THE WAY AS THAT TABLE.`

segments.voice: First, one place for two kinds of people. The chapter calls the Tao the treasure of the good, and in the same breath, what the not-good hold on to for protection. It doesn't keep a separate shelter for each. The good treasure it. The ones who've gone wrong hide in it. Same Way. Second, a question. The chapter asks, more or less: even if people are not good, why should they be thrown away? It doesn't answer with a rule. It leaves the question standing, and the question does the work. Third, the best gift. The chapter pictures a ruler being crowned, with officials appointed and grand presents brought in: a disc of precious jade, a fine team of horses. Better than all of it, the chapter says, would be to sit still and offer this Way. The most valuable thing in the room isn't on a cart. Fourth, why the old ones prized it. The chapter recalls a saying: through the Tao, those who seek will find, and those who have done wrong will escape it. That's the refuge. Not a hiding place from consequences, exactly, but a place where a person who failed isn't finished. In a normal week, that might mean the coworker who blew the deadline, the friend who flaked, or the person in the mirror who did the thing again. The chapter's question follows them all into the room. Why throw anyone away?
screen: `TREASURE AND REFUGE, ONE PLACE.` · `WHY THROW ANYONE AWAY?` · `BETTER THAN JADE AND HORSES.` · then, large: `SEEKERS FIND, THE WRONG ESCAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone who's failed. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one person who has messed up lately. It might be someone close. It might be you. Notice the urge to lecture, or to close the door. You don't have to excuse what happened. Just picture pulling out a chair for them, and setting down a plate. No speech. Stay with that picture for a while. If it's hard, that's fine; let it be hard and keep the chair there anyway. The bell holds the time.
Refuge of the bad. In chapter sixty-two, the Tao is the treasure of the good and the shelter of those who aren't. Today's word.
Your line: a refuge. Find one person today who's had a bad stretch, and make room for them without a lecture. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-two as a teaching that no one is beyond the Way: they keep the door open to people who have failed instead of writing them off.

trapdoor: what you thought: a refuge of the bad sounds like a hideout for criminals.
what it means: the Way still holds people who have gone wrong; nobody is thrown away.
what a scholar hears: the chapter keeps the good and the not-good in one sentence; the same Way is treasure to one and shelter to the other.

notes: Chapter 62 is paraphrased throughout (no quotation) because the writer was not certain of Legge's exact wording.
The chapter mentions 'three ministers' and teams of four horses; the script deliberately leaves out the numbers and says 'officials' and 'a fine team of horses'.
Trapdoor: 奧 (ào) glossed as the deep, sheltered inner (southwest) corner of a house; confirm this lexicon sense and its fit here.
Original 不善人之所保 (bù shàn rén zhī suǒ bǎo) rendered approximately; confirm.
'Those who have done wrong will escape it' paraphrases 有罪以免; check the sense (escape guilt or escape punishment).
The kitchen-table image is the writer's illustration, not the text's.
Editor: cut the trapdoor's lexicon gloss of 奧 (an etymology-style claim the cited text doesn't make) for a line drawn from the chapter itself; replaced the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
